w:r.w:t: DBMS PROJECT LITERATURE REVIEW
1. Proposed Title
A Digital Twin Framework for Real-Time Climate Hazard Monitoring and Early Warning in Urban Critical Infrastructure
(Bridging kilometre-scale climate simulation and asset-scale IoT sensing through data assimilation, surrogate forecasting and graded alerting)
Alternative formulations
CliTwin
: An IoT-Enabled Digital Twin Framework for Real-Time Multi-Hazard Climate Risk Monitoring and Predictive Early Warning
• Real-Time Climate Hazard Monitoring Using a Digital Twin Framework: Data Assimilation, Surrogate Forecasting and Decision Support
• From Earth-System Twins to Asset Twins: A Multi-Scale Architecture for Continuous Climate Hazard Monitoring and Graded Early Warning
2. Background and Motivation

Extreme events of climatic origin — pluvial and coastal flooding, storm surge, heatwaves, wildfire, and the compound cascades that arise when these coincide — are growing more frequent and more severe. Their consequences fall hardest on dense urban regions, where power, water, transport and drainage networks are so tightly coupled that failure in one propagates rapidly into the others. Yet the instruments we use to watch for such failures remain stubbornly fragmented. Meteorological forecasting, structural health monitoring, SCADA telemetry and GIS asset registers are each maintained as a separate system, on separate update cycles, by separate teams. The operational picture is assembled by hand, and usually only once an event is already under way.

A digital twin — a virtual replica held in continuous, bidirectional correspondence with the physical system it represents — is an obvious candidate for integrating these strands. Such a system could ingest live sensor and forecast streams, keep a georeferenced model of exposed assets synchronised with reality, simulate the near-term evolution of a hazard, and translate that simulation into graded warnings carrying a quantified lead time. The concept is not new. What has changed is that the computational and observational infrastructure needed to realise it has, within the last two years, become available.

The difficulty is that the field has developed at two scales that do not yet meet. Destination Earth now operates kilometre-resolution Earth-system twins on exascale hardware [4], [6], [7]. At the opposite extreme, individual studies instrument a single tunnel [1], a single heritage hall [9], or a line of gas sensors along a rural road [3], achieving metre-level fidelity over a domain of a few hundred square metres. Neither reaches the other. An operator who needs to know whether a particular substation, tunnel or drainage inlet will flood within the next two hours is served by a 5 km grid cell no better than by a camera trained on water that has already arrived. Closing that distance, and measuring what it costs to close it, is the problem this project takes up.
3. Research Gap

Eight deficiencies emerge from the literature surveyed in Section 5. Each is stated below with the evidence that supports it and with the reason it has become tractable now, since several of these gaps have persisted less because they were intractable than because the enabling infrastructure did not exist.
A scale gap separates Earth-system twins from asset twins (G1).

Destination Earth resolves the Earth system at 5–10 km over multi-decadal horizons [4], and its extremes twin achieves 4.4 km globally and 500–750 m over Europe [7]. Against this, the asset-level studies resolve a tunnel cross-section in millimetres [1] or place twenty-three gas sensors along eleven miles of road [3]. Only one reviewed demonstrator occupies the intervening band, and it is a scenario tool rather than a monitoring system [10]. Nothing propagates a kilometre-scale hazard forecast into a metre-scale asset consequence. This was until recently impractical for a mundane reason: a downstream system would have had to ingest a petabyte-scale archive to obtain the fields it needed. The Polytope feature-extraction service and the Forecast-in-a-Box prototype [6], together with user-requested on-demand simulation in the extremes twin [7], have made targeted retrieval for a single domain feasible for the first time.
Real-time performance is measured only in fragments (G2).
The best-instrumented study in the set reports transport latency at seconds-scale and dashboard freshness within six
minutes but

offers no runtime whatever for its WRF-GHG-to-large-eddy chain [3]. Another quotes a 15 FPS sensor rate while never timing the reconstruction pipeline that consumes it [1]. Destination Earth reports throughput in simulated years per wall-clock day [4], a figure that describes how fast the model runs rather than how quickly an observation becomes a warning. Not one study publishes an end-to-end observation-to-warning latency. That such a figure is obtainable on a real deployment is precisely what [3] demonstrates; the instrumentation pattern exists and needs extending across the simulation stage rather than inventing from scratch.
Data assimilation is invoked more often than implemented (G3).
One study nominates Kalman filtering or ensemble update schemes as its synchronisation mechanism, then implements a heuristic
SoftMax

–exponential-moving-average reweighting in their place [2]. Another states only that its twin is continuously updated with live sensor data, without specifying any scheme at all [3]. Rigorous assimilation exists at Earth-system scale [4], but it has not been brought down to the scale of an individual asset. Ensemble Kalman implementations are mature and openly available, and [3] already supplies a working broker-and-topic architecture into which a state-update step can be inserted. What is missing is integration, not method.
Validation against real hazard events is largely absent (G4).

The most quantitatively rigorous study in the set validates on a 1:10 laboratory tunnel model, its authors observing candidly that field validation is constrained by the unpredictability and danger of real events [1]. A second is wholly synthetic, so that its reported errors measure self-consistency rather than predictive skill [2]. Four further works are conceptual and report no empirical results at all [8], [9], [12], [13]. Waiting for a live event is not a research strategy. Well-documented recent disasters with open hydro-meteorological records — the July 2021 Zhengzhou rainstorm that motivates [1] among them — combined with the storyline re-simulation capability now operational in [4], permit a hindcast-and-replay protocol that does not depend on chance.
Forecast uncertainty is rarely quantified at asset scale (G5).
None of the implemented asset-
scale

systems [1], [2], [3], [9] reports a confidence interval, an ensemble spread, or any calibration diagnostic. Uncertainty is treated seriously only in the Earth-system twins [4], and there on climate-projection rather than warning timescales. A warning issued without bounds is difficult for an operator to act upon, and the omission is no longer justified by cost: deep-ensemble and quantile methods are computationally cheap once a surrogate exists, and the operational adoption of the Anemoi framework and its sectoral prototypes [6] indicates that surrogate modelling has passed from research prototype into production practice.
Almost every implemented system is descriptive rather than anticipatory (G6).

One measures water that has already entered the tunnel [1]; another detects a leak that is already emitting [3]. A single exception specifies predictive warnings twenty-four to forty-eight hours ahead of a forecast environmental exceedance, though without empirical validation of that horizon [9]. No study in the set measures the lead time it
actually achieves

, or the false-alarm cost of achieving it. Such a measurement now has something to be measured against: [7] publishes upstream forecast horizons of up to four days globally and two days regionally, which together define a lead-time budget within which a downstream warning can be specified and evaluated.
Multi-hazard cascades are formalised but not executed (G7).

One study defines a hazard-transition matrix and a normalised resilience loss-and-recovery function, then realises only the heat–outage–smoke chain [2]. Another argues the case for cascading failures at a conceptual level [13]. Nothing in the surveyed literature runs a genuine cascade on real data. The formal apparatus is therefore available — [2] supplies the algebra, [13] the rationale for operating under partial observability — and the binding constraint has shifted from theory to data access.
Deployment engineering is unevenly addressed (G8).

Only one study presents a validated communication and power stack: MQTT with QoS 1 and session recovery, cellular uplink, packet loss below 0.1%, under 1 kbps per node, solar harvesting, and seventeen months of continuous field operation [3]. A second specifies a cloud–edge–sensor hierarchy in comparable detail but never deploys it [9]. Against these, one study connects a single camera to a laptop over a USB cable [1], and another specifies no stack at all [2]. The field-proven hardware and communication design in [3] can be adopted rather than redesigned, and [9] supplies a complementary edge-gateway pattern for sites with mains power.
4. Aim and Objectives

The aim of this project is to design, implement and validate a multi-scale, bidirectional digital twin framework that couples kilometre-scale meteorological and climate forecasts with asset-scale IoT telemetry and geospatial asset models, so as to monitor climate hazards continuously, forecast their short-horizon evolution with quantified uncertainty, and issue graded early warnings whose end-to-end latency and lead time are measured rather than asserted.
Six objectives follow from this aim.

To survey digital twin architectures across scales, from Earth-system twins to single-asset monitoring systems, and to derive from that survey a formal specification of the functional and non-functional requirements — update latency, forecast horizon, spatial resolution, accuracy and scalability — that a real-time climate hazard twin must satisfy.

To design a layered reference architecture comprising a physical sensing layer, an edge pre-processing layer, a communication layer, a data and model repository, an analytics layer, and a visualisation and decision-support layer, capable of nesting kilometre-scale forecast fields down to metre-scale asset state across a defined study area.

To implement a real-time ingestion and assimilation pipeline — edge filtering, a message broker offering guaranteed delivery, and a formal state-update scheme such as an ensemble Kalman filter — that holds the virtual replica in continuous correspondence with the physical system, and to measure the resulting observation-to-update latency end to end.

To develop and validate a hybrid forecasting engine coupling a reduced-order physics-based hazard model with an AI surrogate, such as an LSTM or a graph neural network ensemble, delivering short-horizon predictions together with calibrated uncertainty bounds expressed as P10–P50–P90 intervals.

To design a multi-level, threshold-driven early-warning and decision-support module that converts twin state and forecast into graded alerts, quantifies the lead time achieved at each level, and supports operator triage through hazard visualisation and what-if scenario replay.

To evaluate the assembled framework against a real historical hazard event, using end-to-end latency, event detection coverage, mean time to detection, warning lead time, forecast skill expressed as RMSE, R², probability of detection and false-alarm ratio, and uncertainty calibration, benchmarked against the baselines identified in the review.

These objectives are written directly against the deficiencies set out above. The first two respond to the scale gap and to the unevenness of deployment engineering (G1, G8), drawing their requirements evidence principally from [7], [10] and [14]. The third addresses the fragmentary treatment of latency and the absence of asset-scale assimilation (G2, G3), building on the communication architecture demonstrated in [3]. The fourth answers the neglect of uncertainty and the descriptive character of existing systems (G5, G6). The fifth converts hazard state into actionable warning, extending the anticipatory pattern of [9] and the human-in-the-loop reasoning of [13] to the cascade formalism of [2] (G6, G7). The last supplies the empirical validation that the field presently lacks (G4).
5. Literature Review
5.1 Approach

Fourteen sources published between 2023 and 2026 form the basis of this review. Three were supplied at the outset of the project [1], [2], [3]; one further source was identified by the project supervisor [6]; the remainder were located through three thematic searches, directed respectively at digital twin frameworks for real-time climate hazard monitoring and early warning, at the Destination Earth programme and its extremes and adaptation twins, and at digital twin applications to urban heat island and heat-health risk. These searches covered the major publisher platforms together with
arXiv
and
returned twenty-five records; with the folder papers and the supervisor's contribution, twenty-nine records were identified in total.

Removing duplicates and mirror records left twenty-four for screening on title and abstract. A source was retained where it proposed, implemented or systematically reviewed a digital twin or an explicitly twin-adjacent system; where it addressed a hazard of climatic or meteorological origin, or contributed an enabling capability directly transferable to one; where it fell within the 2023–2026 window; where its bibliographic details could be verified independently; and where it was published in English. Ten records were set aside. Two lay outside the hazard scope, offering no transferable methodological contribution; two were programme announcements superseded by more recent material from the same source; two could not be obtained in full for verification; two overlapped substantively with a review already retained; and for two, the venue or bibliographic details could not be established with confidence. Fourteen sources were carried forward.

The window was chosen deliberately to capture the current state of the art, at the acknowledged cost of historical depth; a single 2023 systematic review [14] was retained as a pre-period baseline against which the more recent work could be tested. Two of the retained sources are preprints [2], [3] and two are programme documentation rather than research outputs [6], [7]; conclusions resting on these are identified as such where they arise. For one source only the abstract could be obtained, and it is cited accordingly [12]. Since almost every quantitative claim in this literature is self-reported by the study that produced it, and none has been independently replicated, the discussion that follows distinguishes throughout between figures that are internally consistent and traceable, figures whose supporting detail is incomplete, and figures that cannot be traced to a primary source at all.
5.2 Terminology
The term "digital twin" is applied in this literature to systems separated by five orders of magnitude in spatial scale and by an equally wide margin in evidential rigour. Three distinctions are
needed, and
are used consistently hereafter.

An Earth-system twin operates at kilometre scale over continental to global domains, forced by numerical weather prediction or climate models, and produces hazard fields rather than asset states; the Destination Earth components are the exemplars [4], [7]. An asset twin operates at metre scale, is bound to a single physical asset or a small sensor network, and produces asset state rather than hazard fields [1], [3], [9]. Between them sits the class this project proposes, and which the survey finds unoccupied: a hazard twin, coupling the two
so as to
ingest Earth-system forcing alongside asset telemetry and emit a timed, graded warning for a specific asset.

A second distinction, taken from the taxonomy of [14], separates a digital shadow — in which data flow only from physical to virtual, with neither observation-driven state correction nor any return path — from a genuinely bidirectional twin, which adds assimilation that corrects the virtual state against incoming observations together with a command or decision path back to the physical system. The distinction is not pedantic. Judged against it, most of the systems reviewed below are shadows.
5.3 Earth
-system and continental-scale climate twins
Destination Earth: the climate change adaptation twin [4]

The Climate Change Adaptation Digital Twin is the most operationally mature system in this review by a considerable margin, and it establishes what the term can mean at the upper limit of ambition. Three global Earth-system models — ICON, IFS-NEMO and IFS-FESOM — run under unified workflow management, with real-time quality monitoring supplied by the AQUA and OBSALL components, sectoral applications embedded to consume streamed output, standardised HEALPix grids, one-pass algorithms for statistical reduction, and tiered storage bridging HPC and cloud through the
DestinE
data lake. Simulations proceed at nominal resolutions of 5–10 km with hourly atmospheric output on the
EuroHPC

pre-exascale systems LUMI and MareNostrum5, covering 1990 to 2040 under SSP3-7.0, at approximately 0.5 simulated years per wall-clock day at 5 km and two to three at 10 km, generating on the order of 100 GB per simulated day per model.

Two capabilities bear on the present project. The twin produces high-resolution storylines in which observed extreme events are re-simulated under alternative climate states, so that a hurricane's precipitation can be quantified across scenarios — a range of 247–271 mm is reported, though this is a model output described narratively rather than an observation, and the underlying figure warrants direct inspection before the range is quoted in a thesis. More consequentially, sectoral applications in energy, water and forest management translate raw climate fields into impact indicators through co-design with users, and this is the nearest analogue in the literature to the hazard-to-asset chain the proposed framework must construct.

The authors are forthright about what remains undone. Higher-frequency output requested by some applications is not yet possible; streaming windows currently extend to a year and are expected to shorten to weeks; GPU porting and energy efficiency remain in progress. The deeper limitation is one of physics rather than engineering. A 5 km grid cannot resolve an individual substation, tunnel or drainage inlet, and a multi-decadal projection is not a live warning. This is adaptation information, and it is excellent of its kind — but the space beneath it is exactly where the present work sits.
Destination Earth: programme rationale [5]
The founding rationale for
Destine

was set out three years earlier: a digital twin of the Earth system merging advanced physical modelling with impact science through new digital technologies, with climate adaptation and disaster management named as the primary objectives of its first phase. The emphasis throughout falls on co-design with stakeholders across renewable resources, water, food, energy and public health, and on mechanisms that allow user communities to build their own applications atop shared information infrastructure. No case study is
presented,

and no quantitative results are reported, so the paper is appropriately cited for the programme's intent and governance model rather than for any measured capability. Its value here lies in establishing that Europe's flagship climate twin was conceived from the outset as a service layer for downstream applications — which is precisely the interface through which an infrastructure-scale hazard twin would draw its forcing. The
emphasis on sectoral co-design also anticipates, by three years, the participatory requirements later formalised in [10].
Destination Earth: current operational status [6]

A programme update of December 2025 provides the most recent account of what the European twins do in practice. Two production twins are confirmed — Climate Change Adaptation and Weather-induced Extremes — running across the Euro
HPC systems LUMI, MareNostrum5, Leonardo,
Melu Xina
and JUPITER, the last described as the first exascale machine in Europe. Simulations at 5 km reach roughly 120 simulated days per day of computation, and the system produces
in excess of

a petabyte of information daily, with climate projections now extending to 2050. This throughput figure sits in mild tension with the 0.5 simulated years per wall-clock day reported in [4], which corresponds to something closer to 183 simulated days per day; the two are of the same order but refer to different dates and configurations, and each ought to be quoted with its source attached rather than treated as interchangeable.

Three developments here matter more than the headline numbers. The Anemoi open-source machine-learning framework, together with prototypes for waves, hydrology, land, ocean and sea ice, shows that surrogate modelling has moved into operational practice — which underwrites both the hybrid approach proposed in Objective 4 and the feasibility argument attached to G5. The Forecast-in-a-Box prototype points toward on-demand, user-triggered simulation, the mechanism by which a local twin would request forcing for its own domain. And the Polytope service, whose feature-extraction functionality permits retrieval of only the specific data required, answers the bandwidth problem that a downstream system would otherwise face against a petabyte-per-day source. Of everything surveyed here, this is the single development that most directly makes the scale gap addressable. Being a programme communication, the update carries no methodology and no validation, and its figures describe current operational status rather than experimental results.
Destination Earth: the weather-induced extremes twin [7]

This is the most important upstream dependency for the proposed framework, and its published specifications alter the project's feasibility calculus. The extremes twin is organised in three layers: Earth-system models, comprising a global component built on ECMWF's Integrated Forecasting System at 4.4 km producing forecasts up to four days ahead, and a regional European component at 500–750 m producing forecasts up to two days ahead, built on the ACCORD system developed by
Météo

-France with thirty-two partner institutions across more than twenty countries; impact-sector models covering floods, air quality and renewable energy; and observations fused with simulation output. Global simulations are initialised daily from operational analysis, and users holding upgraded platform access may request both routine and on-demand simulations. Data retrieval proceeds through the Polytope service and a Harmonised Data Access API covering the past fifteen start dates. Tropical cyclones, heavy rainfall and deep convective systems are among the phenomena addressed.

A regional field at 500–750 m is close enough to urban scale to drive an asset-level twin without the interpolation error a 5 km field would introduce, and this is the concrete basis for treating G1 as newly tractable. The published forecast horizons matter equally: four days globally and two days regionally define an upstream lead-time budget, giving the warning-lead-time metric in Objective 6 something measurable to be evaluated against. That a flood impact-sector model already exists upstream means the first stage of hazard-to-impact translation need not be rebuilt. Set against this, the caveats

are those of any programme resource. No validation statistics or forecast skill scores are published; no request-to-delivery latency is stated for on-demand simulation; access to that capability is gated on platform privileges; and the fifteen-start-date retention window will constrain any hindcast study requiring a longer archive.
5.4 Asset
-scale monitoring twins
Real-time three-dimensional monitoring of subway tunnel waterlogging [1]

Of the asset-scale studies surveyed, this is the most rigorously measured and the closest in hazard framing to the proposed work. Its motivation is the Zhengzhou rainstorm of 20 July 2021, in which flooding of Metro Line 5 caused mass fatalities in underground spaces. The Physics-Digitization-Intelligence Fusion System comprises three layers: a physical space in which an Azure Kinect captures RGB, depth and infrared streams over a USB 4.0 link; a digital twin layer reconstructing a dynamic point cloud updated continuously as data arrive; and an intelligent operations layer that fits the water surface by RANSAC, derives per-point depth by point-to-plane distance, integrates volume from tunnel geometry, and computes flow rate from the rate of volume change. Because depth sensing is infrared, the system functions in complete darkness — the condition under which camera-based methods ordinarily fail, and a genuine contribution.

Validation on a 1:10 concrete model of the Zhengzhou tunnel, 0.62 m in outer diameter with a 30‰ gradient and injection at 40–60 L/min, yields a mean depth accuracy of 99.12% with a mean absolute error of 1.09 mm; volume accuracy of 96.09% under illumination and 94.27% in darkness; and flow-rate accuracy of 98.58% and 96.01% respectively. A refraction compensation regression,
Ht

= 1.001Hr + 51.19 with R² = 0.9474, reduces large-depth tank error from a mean of 56 mm to 9 mm. Robustness testing shows depth shifts of only 0.1–1.3 mm under noise injection, 5% data dropout, occlusion, reflection, turbulence and varying illumination, with sensitivity to assumed radius and slope bounded within ±3.4%. Two qualifications attach to these figures. The headline depth accuracy is obtained under illumination, since the paper acknowledges that RGB scale references were unavailable in darkness and dark-condition depth accuracy is therefore inferred rather than measured; and the reported accuracies aggregate two experimental runs compared at ten-second intervals, without repetition counts, confidence intervals or statistical testing.

The limitations that matter most are structural rather than a question of execution quality, which is high. The system is descriptive: it measures water that has already entered one cross-section of one tunnel. There is no rainfall, meteorological or hydrological forcing, no coupling to the drainage network, no forecast and consequently no lead time — the clearest single instance of the descriptive-not-anticipatory problem. Nor is there any system integration layer: no IoT protocol, no server, no database, no dashboard, no alerting logic, no multi-node network. The deployment is one camera on a cable to a computer. And despite real-time operation being the central claim, no pipeline latency or per-frame processing time is reported, only the 15 FPS rate of the sensor itself. The authors state plainly that field validation remains constrained by the unpredictability and hazard of real events, and that judgement seems fair.
AIMNET: continuous gas emission monitoring and early hazard detection [3]

This is the only reviewed study with a sustained real-world deployment, and its engineering discipline makes it the natural template for the sensing and communication layers of the proposed framework. The physical layer is a custom non-dispersive-infrared gas sensing device built on an application-
specific PCB — an Adafruit Feather M0 controller, a SIM7070G narrow-band cellular modem, a solar harvesting module — deliberately avoiding development boards in order to reduce power draw and unit
cost, and
achieving 1404
mW

against the 8–41 W of the LI-7700 reference instrument, with a week of operation between charges. Communication runs over a self-hosted MQTT broker assigning a unique topic per device, selected over HTTP and CoAP for its acknowledgment and session-recovery semantics, and carrying downlink reconfiguration commands as well as uplink data, with application-layer encryption and a honeypot for intrusion detection. The twin layer hosts a regression-based calibration model correcting for humidity, temperature and drift; a WRF-GHG regional weather-and-greenhouse-gas simulation nested into a geometry-resolving large-eddy simulation; anomaly detection with neighbour-based imputation; Kafka and Spark for stream processing; and a dashboard synchronising geospatial maps with time series.

Twenty-three devices were mounted on power posts across the Anadarko Basin at roughly 2.5 m height and half-mile spacing, operating continuously from March 2024 to July 2025, with a mobile campaign at the City of Norman Water Reclamation Facility benchmarked against an LI-7700. Reported performance includes approximately 90% of the reference instrument's leak-detection accuracy, reliable identification above 5 ppm, and a single false positive at 15 ppm; calibration to within about ±3 ppm, with R² of 0.948 indoors and 0.908 outdoors; packet loss below 0.1% at average uplink bandwidth under 1 kbps per node; and a multiscale chain running WRF-GHG at 32 m nested into a 5 m large-eddy simulation, which resolves plume meandering the coarser model cannot. That 90% accuracy figure should be handled with some care: no denominator, event count or confusion matrix accompanies it, and the evidence
actually presented
consists of one false positive and one missed zone. The claim is plausible but not, as published, reproducible.

What sets this study apart is a single number that no other reviewed work provides. A five-minute sampling window followed by a one-minute uplink yields dashboard freshness within six minutes, with transport latency once sent measured at seconds-scale. This is the kind of quantity the proposed framework must produce for a complete hazard chain, and it is the reason G2 can be treated as an engineering problem rather than an open research question. Much nonetheless remains undone. There is no formal assimilation — the twin is simply said to be continuously updated. Inverse modelling and source localisation are described but never executed or evaluated. No forecast horizon or lead time is reported, so the system detects rather than anticipates. The physics chain carries no runtime, meaning the real-time claim covers the network alone and not the simulation. And seventeen months of data from twenty-three nodes are nowhere analysed, validation resting instead on short mobile transects.
A digital twin for architectural heritage [9]

This study earns its place for one reason above all others: it is the only reviewed work that specifies anticipatory action with an explicit time bound. Predictive warnings are triggered twenty-four to forty-eight hours ahead of a forecast environmental exceedance, and pre-emptive dehumidification is initiated a full day before a predicted threshold breach. Given that no other system in the survey reports a lead time at all, this supplies the design pattern the early-warning module of Objective 5 requires, even though the hazard class differs from those of primary interest.

Five components sit over a hierarchical cloud–edge–sensor architecture built on an HBIM foundation, with STM32 sensor nodes, Raspberry Pi gateways, MQTT transmission to the cloud, and web-based visualisation. Structural health monitoring draws on hydrostatic levellers for settlement, corner-

mounted tilt sensors, vibrating-wire displacement meters and photogrammetry with AI-based crack detection, feeding finite-element stress analysis calibrated against modal measurements. Microclimate monitoring covers temperature, humidity, CO₂, PM1.0, illuminance and wind speed, with Bluetooth Low-Energy RSSI fingerprinting for occupancy and predictive control by GRU time-series models and CFD-informed radial basis function networks. Energy management combines smart metering,
Energy Plus
simulation and an automated retrofit evaluation tool. The application case is
Dacheng
Hall of the
Xiangyi
Confucian Temple, a Qing Dynasty structure of 1744 and 1880 covering 420 m² in a subtropical humid climate.
The cross-domain coupling is the second idea worth carrying forward. Predictive humidity models inform dehumidification timing
so as to

slow material deterioration; occupancy patterns sharpen both environmental and structural stress prediction; CFD-identified risk zones guide HVAC placement to protect vulnerable elements. Here is a worked example of the impact chain that G7 finds missing elsewhere. Its limitations, however, govern how it can be cited. The authors position the work explicitly as a design research study producing a conceptual framework rather than an empirical validation, and no empirical results are reported; the 25–55% energy saving figure is drawn from prior literature, not measured here. The hazard addressed is chronic environmental stress — mould risk above 75% relative humidity, thermal cycling, differential settlement — rather than an acute climatic event, and the retrofit tool is stated to require professional
EnergyPlus
expertise, which bounds its operational transferability.
A digital-twin platform for
cryospheric
disaster warning [8]

This perspective addresses a hazard class the remaining studies omit entirely: glacier-related disasters intensified by warming, encompassing glacial lake outburst floods, ice-rock avalanches and glacial debris flows. The proposed platform integrates multisource data management across remote sensing, seismic and geophone networks and meteorological stations; physics-based numerical models combined with machine learning; supercomputing infrastructure; and virtual-reality interfaces for visualisation and decision support. Its most transferable contribution is a three-phase operating cycle — hindcasting for historical analysis, forecasting for probabilistic risk assessment, nowcasting for real-time event simulation with dynamic parameter updating — which maps cleanly onto the monitoring, prediction and warning functions of the proposed framework and supplies the structure for the hindcast-and-replay validation protocol advanced against G4.

It remains, however, a perspective: no case study, no dataset, no quantitative result. The barriers its authors identify are a useful corrective to optimism about field deployment. Monitoring networks in high-mountain terrain are sparse; instruments are not optimised for those conditions; data sharing across national borders is restricted; deployment environments are physically punishing; specialised workforce training is scarce. These are the same constraints that lead [13] to argue for designing under partial observability rather than assuming complete telemetry.
5.5 Urban
-scale, multi-hazard and participatory frameworks
A hazard-responsive digital twin for urban resilience and equity [2]

This is the most ambitious conceptual design in the review and the only work to place social equity inside the twin rather than beside it. Three layers are specified: a physical layer of fixed and mobile sensors supplemented by UAV, satellite and, where infrastructure sensing fails, crowd-sourced and volunteered geographic information; a digital-intelligence layer fusing physics-informed neural

networks, finite-element surrogates and reinforcement-learning modules; and a decision layer presenting probabilistic forecasts, uncertainty maps and social-equity indicators. Compounding hazards are formalised through weighted hazard superposition with reinforcement-learned importance weights, a logistic hazard-transition matrix, and a normalised resilience loss-and-recovery function. Physics enters through a 2R2C lumped thermal model with a smoke-modulated ventilation term, embedded in a physics-informed neural network loss balancing data fidelity against the PDE residual. Equity is handled by a node-level index weighting physical vulnerability at 0.6 and socio-economic sensitivity at 0.4, aggregated into a population-weighted urban index with a disadvantage amplifier.

The demonstration is a synthetic district of 120 buildings across six archetypes, simulated over seventy-two hours at ten-minute steps under a wildfire-outage-heatwave cascade, with roughly a tenth of nodes carrying IoT temperature sensors subject to outage-induced dropout, alongside hourly UAV and six-hourly satellite observations. The physics-informed network attains an overall RMSE of 1.93 °C and MAE of 1.42 °C, improving to 1.60 °C for IoT-driven predictions, and reproduces blackout-driven indoor peaks of 31–33 °C. Prospective interventions reduce population-weighted thermal risk by 11–13%, tail risk by 7–17% and overheating hours by up to 9%, with a Pareto analysis identifying the strongest option at −12.9% and −16.9% respectively.

Both sets of figures require careful reading. The study is wholly synthetic, and its virtual measurements are generated from the same prescribed latent temperature process against which the network is subsequently validated; the reported errors therefore quantify self-consistency, not predictive skill. The intervention percentages propagate hand-set exposure multipliers of 0.70, 0.65 and 0.50 through the risk equation, which makes them a form of assumption-propagation rather than measurement. There is, besides, a marked distance between architecture and implementation. Kalman or ensemble assimilation, finite-element surrogates, LiDAR, SCADA, social sensing, the hazard-transition matrix, the resilience function and the PM2.5 balance are all specified; none is exercised in the case study, where only the 2R2C model
actually runs

. No uncertainty quantification is reported, despite uncertainty maps being a stated decision-layer output, and no latency or streaming implementation exists — the authors themselves list real-time assimilation, scalability and field validation among their future priorities. The work is best treated as a design target and a source of formalism, particularly the equity weighting and the compounding-hazard algebra invoked under G7, rather than as demonstrated capability.
A participatory framework for actionable climate adaptation modelling [10]
This paper contributes something no other reviewed work does: empirical evidence, rather than assertion, about what users
actually require

of a climate digital twin. The Generic Adaptation Modelling Framework comprises eight steps across three phases — a scoping phase led by end-users, in which a problem or vision is defined, the system understood, drivers of risk and impact identified, and adaptation measures curated; a co-development phase led by technical developers, covering software selection, data collection and pre-processing, workflow construction and post-processing routines; and a use phase of scenario exploration and iterative refinement. Four principles govern the whole: co-production of knowledge, modularity, transparency, iteration. Three user groups are distinguished — developers, end-users and civil society.
The requirements evidence is the substantive contribution. A tiered engagement strategy involved twenty-five Tier-1 stakeholders through one-to-one interviews and more than four hundred Tier-2

stakeholders through webinars and external events, yielding 441 discrete user stories that were translated into 128 unique system requirements across seventeen thematic groups. Technical requirements dominated at 70.3%, with cross-cutting contextual concerns — participation, equity, policy integration — accounting for 21.1% and framework design elements 8.6%. The single most frequently expressed requirement, at eighty-three mentions, was to select modular, interoperable modelling tools; the second, at seventy-two, was to analyse which hazards, exposures and vulnerabilities are relevant. For a proposal whose second objective is a layered, modular reference architecture, this constitutes direct empirical justification rather than a stylistic preference. These are, necessarily, self-reported process metrics that cannot be externally audited, but they are transparently derived and internally consistent.
Two demonstrators ground the framework. Heat stress adaptation in the Basque Country applies the
UrbClim

model at 100 m resolution across nine urban areas over 2001–2020, with a neural network upscaling results region-wide from surface characteristics and outputs joined to epidemiological data and health determinants. Coastal flood risk at Scheveningen uses hydrodynamic models of future storm surge under sea-level rise to evaluate structural measures such as surge barriers. The 100 m heat demonstrator carries particular significance here, since it occupies precisely the resolution band between Earth-system twins and asset twins that G1 identifies as empty, and shows that the band is reachable with tools already in hand.

The definition of a digital twin advanced in this paper is also stricter than most implementations meet: virtual models updated with real-time data, requiring interactive modelling in which users define and test scenarios, and therefore requiring tools that automatically generate, update and validate model schematisations from user inputs. Measured against that bar,
the majority of

systems reviewed here would not qualify. The authors' own limitations are stated candidly: engagement skewed toward government, research and consultancy actors, so that the needs of grassroots and community-based organisations may not be fully captured, particularly outside EU contexts; a framework demanding time, coordination and capacity that may simply not be available; demonstrators that exposed the technical complexity of integrating modular tools and the time cost of accessing and harmonising high-resolution climate data; and use cases not yet mature enough, in their words, to yield evidence regarding adaptation outcomes.
Digital twins for urban heat monitoring and policy integration [11]

A PRISMA 2020 review of Web of Science and Scopus across 2010–2025 screened 356 records and analysed 96, proposing a hexagonal capability framework that spans sensing and monitoring, data integration and processing, the twin engine, analytics and AI, visualisation and decision support, and policy integration, realised over four layers: physical, communication, data processing and application. Inputs range across IoT sensor networks, satellite thermal imagery, building management systems and social sensing platforms, with Dhaka supplying the applied context, where heat-related economic losses are put at 8% of city GDP.

The review's usefulness lies in the benchmark figures it draws from its corpus, and here a distinction must be drawn firmly. These are figures reported by a review about the studies within it; the primary sources are not identified in the accessible record, and they are consequently not traceable. They should be cited as reported in the review literature and never as the performance of a named system. On that understanding, the corpus reports hybrid deep-learning models attaining 94% accuracy in forecasting urban heat exposure, spatial resolution improved from 1.5 km grids to 100 m, emergency

response times 27% faster than conventional strategies, cost reductions of 20–30%, and urban heat island differentials of 4–10 °C. One figure proves more useful than the others: reviewed systems achieving sub-kilometre predictions at 10–30 second update frequencies, which is the only concrete update-rate target encountered anywhere in this literature and is adopted here as a design reference for Objective 3. The barriers the review identifies — data integration complexity, governance, interoperability, and six to twelve months of calibration before a twin becomes reliable — are a salutary corrective to any assumption that such a system can be stood up quickly. The review contains no implementation of its own, and notes that review papers constitute only 7.3% of its corpus, which it reads as evidence of absent standardised protocols and cross-case comparison.
Digital twin technology for urban heat island mitigation [12]

This systematic review consolidates digital twin applications to urban heat island mitigation from twenty-four retrieved materials, proposing REFLECT — a seven-layer framework comprising Retrieve, Establish, Facilitate, Lump, Examine, Cognition and Take — which specifies inputs, processes and outputs for a multilayered mitigation platform, and classifying the literature into three groups: digital-twin-enabled optimisation of urban greenery, digital twin implementation for urban resilience, and enhancement of twin fidelity for heat island applications.

It is cited here for a specific evidential purpose. Alongside [11], it is the second independent systematic review to conclude that urban heat digital twins remain framework-level, with fragmented knowledge and no consolidated implementation evidence. Two independent reviews converging on the same finding constitutes materially stronger support for G4 than either would provide alone, and the convergence is worth more than either framework in isolation. An honest qualification must accompany the citation: only the abstract could be obtained, so the screening dates, database list, inclusion criteria and any quantitative findings remain unverified. The work is therefore cited for its framework and for that convergence, and it should be re-examined in full before the complete proposal is submitted.
The digital risk twin for disaster risk management [13]

The argument advanced here is that the standard digital twin assumption — fully automated sensing coupled to automated intervention — breaks down in disaster settings, where infrastructure is degraded, sensor coverage is partial, and much of what determines vulnerability is socio-cultural and cannot be sensed at all. The proposed Digital Risk Twin retains the three constituents of a twin but redefines each. Data collection becomes hybrid, combining IoT and remote sensing with UAV survey, crowdsourcing, social media and field observation. Decision-making becomes human-in-the-loop, the twin informing rather than executing interventions. Adaptation becomes context-sensitive, functioning without complete sensor infrastructure. Agent-based modelling of evacuation behaviour, AI-based image recognition on UAV and satellite imagery, and continuous model updating are discussed as methods, and the framework is illustrated through a hypothetical earthquake, landslide and cascading-failure scenario inspired by the 2023
Kahramanmaraş
earthquakes, spanning preparedness, early warning, response, recovery and resilience.

For the present project this is a necessary counterweight to the engineering-led studies, and it converges with the field constraints reported in [8] and with the participation requirements evidenced in [10]. It supplies a defensible justification for designing under partial observability and degraded communications rather than assuming ideal telemetry, and it is among the few reviewed works to

treat cascading multi-hazard chains explicitly. Its limitations are those of any conceptual contribution — no implementation, no dataset, no quantitative evaluation — and the barriers it names, computational demand, integration complexity, privacy and security risk, infrastructure and training cost, are identified rather than resolved.
Digital twins, 3D city modelling and early warning systems for climate resilience [14]

A PRISMA systematic review of Web of Science, ScienceDirect and IEEE Xplore across 2010–2021 screened 1,601 records down to 68 papers containing 37 case studies, classified as 10 digital twin frameworks, 14 3D city models and 13 early warning systems, and covering coastal flooding, storm surge, landslides, tsunamis, sea-level rise, heavy precipitation and erosion. The enabling stack is documented in detail:
CityGML
CityJSON

, SketchUp and ArcGIS across LOD0–LOD4; LIDAR, photogrammetry, UAV imagery and terrestrial laser scanning; rainfall, water-level, tiltmeter, temperature-humidity, crack and tide-gauge sensors over GSM/4G;
WebGIS

with cloud analytics driving three-tier green-orange-red alerting. The classification arithmetic is internally consistent, though the country breakdown offered for the case studies — China seven, the United States four, Spain and Taiwan three apiece — accounts for seventeen of thirty-seven and should be read as a partial listing rather than a complete distribution.

The review's most consequential contribution is definitional, and it is the source of the shadow-versus-twin distinction adopted earlier in this chapter. Separating unidirectional data flows, digital shadows and genuinely bidirectional twins, the authors conclude that the field remains primarily in the phase of theoretical concepts and discussion, with substantial gaps in the implementation of bidirectional data flow. Alerting, they find, is still overwhelmingly one-way, and adoption concentrated in high-income regions — a geographic skew that this review's English-language restriction can only compound. Because its coverage terminates in 2021, the work serves here as the baseline against which the 2023–2026 studies are tested, and that test is the substance of the synthesis below.
5.7 Synthesis
Four patterns emerge from the survey, and together they define the space this project occupies.

The literature is stratified by scale, with a sparsely occupied band between its two poles. At the upper end, Destination Earth runs kilometre-resolution Earth-system twins on exascale hardware, producing over a petabyte a day [6], with an extremes twin reaching 4.4 km globally and 500–750 m regionally [7]. At the lower end, asset twins resolve a tunnel cross-section to about a millimetre [1], instrument a single heritage hall [9], or distribute twenty-three gas sensors along eleven miles of road [3]. Only one reviewed demonstrator occupies the intervening band — the 100 m
UrbClim

heat model in [10] — and it is a scenario tool rather than an operational monitoring system. The operator who asks whether a particular substation will flood in the next two hours is served by none of them.

Where real-time performance is concerned, the evidence is fragmentary and the fragments do not join up. The strongest case reports transport latency at seconds-scale and dashboard freshness within six
minutes, yet

supplies no runtime at all for its coupled weather and large-eddy simulation [3]. Another quotes a 15 FPS sensor rate while never timing the reconstruction pipeline it feeds [1]. The Earth-system twins report throughput in simulated years per wall-clock day [4] — a measure of how fast the model runs, not of how quickly an observation becomes a warning, and one that does not even agree exactly with the throughput reported elsewhere by the same programme [6]. No reviewed study
publishes an end-to-end observation-to-warning latency, which is the single figure an operational hazard
twin
most needs
in order to
defend itself.

The definitional gap identified in 2023 has closed only partially. That review found bidirectional data flow largely unrealised [14]; three years later a genuine downlink command path does exist at device level [3], and operational twins do exist at Earth-system scale [4], [6], [7]. But no reviewed system assimilates observations to correct the state of an asset-scale model. One nominates Kalman or ensemble filtering and implements heuristic reweighting in its stead [2]; another states only that its twin is continuously updated [3]. At asset scale, the digital shadow of [14]'s taxonomy remains the norm, and the conclusion that review reached in 2023 still stands for this class of system in 2026.

Nearly every implemented system, finally, is descriptive rather than anticipatory, and validation against real hazard events is thin. The rigorous studies measure consequences already realised [1], [3]; the anticipatory ones are synthetic [2] or conceptual [8], [9], [12], [13]. The one exception specifies a
twenty-four to forty-eight hour
predictive warning but reports no empirical validation of it [9]. Not a single study measures the lead time it
actually achieves

. Where uncertainty is quantified seriously, it is at climate-projection scale [4] rather than at the horizon on which an evacuation or a service suspension must be decided. Two independent systematic reviews converge on this diagnosis [11], [12], which lends it more weight than either would carry alone.

The proposed work therefore addresses an integration and evidentiary gap rather than a deficiency in hazard modelling as such. What is envisaged is a twin that draws kilometre-scale forcing from operational sources — made practical for the first time by the Polytope feature-extraction service and the Forecast-in-a-Box prototype [6], together with the on-demand simulation capability of the extremes twin [7] — assimilates live asset telemetry to correct its own state, forecasts with calibrated uncertainty, warns with a lead time measured against the upstream horizons published in [7], and validates against a real event using the hindcast-forecast-nowcast protocol set out in [8]. Every component has been demonstrated somewhere in this literature. None of it has yet been demonstrated as a closed loop.
5.8 Limitations
of the review

Several constraints qualify the conclusions above. This is a structured narrative review rather than a systematic one: identification, screening and extraction were performed by a single reviewer, without a second screener or any inter-rater agreement check, so selection and extraction bias cannot be excluded. The counts reported in Section 5.1 are offered for auditability, not as a claim of PRISMA compliance. The search itself was structured but not exhaustive — three thematic searches rather than full Boolean queries across Scopus, Web of Science and IEEE Xplore, with no systematic sweep of grey literature, non-indexed proceedings or reference-list snowballing. Relevant work almost certainly exists beyond the twenty-four records screened.

Four of the fourteen retained sources lack peer review: two preprints [2], [3] and two programme communications [6], [7]. This is a material dependency, since [3] supplies the strongest real-time evidence in the review and [7] underpins the feasibility argument for both G1 and G6. Conclusions resting on these four are flagged where they arise, but they should be revisited should peer-reviewed versions appear. Access was also uneven. Full text could not be obtained for [12], which is cited with that restriction stated, and two further records were set aside at screening for the same reason — an
availability bias rather than a quality judgement, and one that institutional access should resolve before the full proposal is submitted.

The 2023–2026 window was chosen deliberately to capture the current state of the art, and the cost is historical depth: foundational earlier work on digital twins, data assimilation and early warning systems falls outside it, and a single retained baseline [14] is no substitute. The restriction to English-language sources is likely to under-represent Chinese-language deployment
literature in particular, which

matters given that [14] locates implementation predominantly in China and [11] draws its applied context from Bangladesh. No formal quality-appraisal instrument was applied, so the relative weight assigned to each source reflects a considered judgement of its evidential strength rather than a reproducible score.

None of this, however, undermines the central finding, which rests on absences rather than on contested figures. No reviewed source publishes an end-to-end observation-to-warning latency, an asset-scale assimilation scheme, or a measured warning lead time. A wider search would be considerably more likely to strengthen that conclusion than to overturn it — but it should be undertaken nonetheless before the full proposal goes forward.
